# Executor

An executor runs the work of a node. Rimsky dispatches a node by calling `Executor.Execute` once and reading the outcome you return.

Two services make up the guide. `Executor` carries the one dispatch RPC. `ExecutorObservability` carries your advertisement and your trace surface, and you serve it from the same process on the same endpoint. Implement `Executor` alone and rimsky still dispatches to you, but the deployment learns nothing about your attributes, your tags, or your error classes.

Proto files: `executor.proto`, `executor_observability.proto`.

## The RPCs

| RPC | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| `Executor.Execute(ExecuteRequest) → Outcome` | Unary |
| `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities(ExecutorCapabilitiesRequest) → ObservabilityCapabilities` | Unary |
| `ExecutorObservability.GetTrace(GetTraceRequest) → Trace` | Unary |
| `ExecutorObservability.StreamTrace(StreamTraceRequest) → stream TraceEvent` | Server streaming |

`Executor` declares no `Capabilities` RPC. Your advertisement lives on the observability sibling.

## Advertising yourself

Rimsky calls `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities` at startup, against the `executors.<name>.observability_endpoint` the operator declared. It caches everything you return and serves it back to operators at `GET /v1/observability/executors`. One declared endpoint is all a deployment needs to know about you.

`ObservabilityCapabilities` fields:

| Field | What rimsky does with it |
| --- | --- |
| `expected_attributes_schema` | JSON Schema bytes. Rimsky validates every registering template's node attributes against it. |
| `declared_tags` | The tag vocabulary template authors may filter subscriptions on. |
| `declared_error_classes` | The error-class vocabulary template authors may route on. |
| `supports_trace_get` | Whether rimsky offers `GetTrace` reads for your dispatches. |
| `supports_trace_stream` | Whether rimsky offers `StreamTrace` reads. |
| `retention_after_terminal_seconds` | How long you keep a trace after its dispatch settles. |
| `http_bridge_url` | Recorded and republished on the observability read routes. Rimsky never dials it. |
| `custom_ui` | A URL and embed mode an operator dashboard can link or frame. |
| `validation_supported_roles` | The roles you answer on the `Validation` mix-in, if you serve it. |

Your advertisement is enforced at template registration, not discovered at dispatch. A node declaring a property your schema types differently is rejected. A node declaring a property your closed schema does not carry is rejected as undeclared. An `error_types` key naming a class outside your vocabulary comes back as a warning. A subscription filtering on a tag you never declared is rejected, and the refusal names both the sending node and your executor.

Leave `expected_attributes_schema` empty and you accept any attributes.

## The dispatch request

`ExecuteRequest` fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `node_id` | The node being run |
| `instance_id` | The instance the node belongs to |
| `node_type` | The node's declared type string |
| `attributes` | The node's resolved attributes, as a `google.protobuf.Struct` |
| `attributes_schema` | The schema those attributes were validated against |
| `claim_producers` | Map from claim alias to `ClaimProducerHandle` — what the node acquired |
| `callback_url` | Base URL of the supervisor's callback listener |
| `cancel_token` | Bearer token for the per-run callback routes |
| `dispatch_id` | This dispatch's id; the key your traces are stored under |
| `run_scope_id` | The execution context this dispatch runs in |
| `prior_dispatch_id` | The previous dispatch of this node, when there was one |
| `prior_dispatch_disposition` | Why the previous dispatch ended |
| `scratch` | Opaque bytes you returned on the previous dispatch |

`prior_dispatch_disposition` takes four values: `PRIOR_NONE`, `PRIOR_STALE_RECOVERY`, `PRIOR_RETRY_AFTER_ERROR`, `PRIOR_RECALCULATE`. Read it to tell a first run from a retry, a recovery, and a recalculation.

`scratch` is yours. Rimsky stores the bytes you return on a `Success`, `Error`, or `Park` outcome and hands them back on the node's next dispatch. It never inspects them. Use it to resume a parked run.

Each `ClaimProducerHandle` carries `kind`, a `handle` struct holding what the producer returned on `Open`, and `candidate_handle` bytes when a data-processing producer opened a candidate. The producer's address, scope, and payload reach you through this map, so store-specific detail arrives without the template author knowing anything about the store.

Fields `userdata` (4), `resumed` (10), `run_attempt` (11), and `resume_context` (13) are reserved. Do not send them.

## The outcome

`Outcome` is a oneof over four cases. Set exactly one.

### Success

Settles the node fresh.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `changed` | Whether this run changed anything downstream |
| `change_summary` | A short human-readable note |
| `attributes_delta` | Attributes to merge onto the node's record |
| `tags` | Terminal tags downstream subscriptions filter on |
| `scratch` | Opaque bytes returned to your next dispatch |

Your `attributes_delta` reaches the graph, so what you computed becomes the node's record.

### Error

Settles the node failed, routed by class.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `error_class` | The class the template's `error_types` policy routes on |
| `payload` | Your own structured error data, passed through uninspected |
| `attributes_delta` | Attributes to merge onto the node's record |
| `tags` | Terminal tags |
| `scratch` | Opaque bytes returned to your next dispatch |

Rimsky matches `error_class` exactly against the template's `error_types` keys and applies the policy it finds: `pass`, `give_up`, `retry`, or `release_and_requeue`. Declare your classes in `declared_error_classes` so template authors can write policies against them.

### Park

Suspends the node instead of settling it.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `resume_at` | When rimsky should resume the node. Required. |
| `tags` | Terminal tags |
| `scratch` | Opaque bytes returned when the node resumes |

A `Park` with no `resume_at` fails the dispatch with the error class `executor_protocol_violation` and the reason `park_missing_resume_at`.

Fields `reason` (1), `payload` (2), `session_token` (4), `reason_note` (5), `reason_label` (6), and `attributes_delta` (8) are reserved on `Park`. Carry your resume state in `scratch`.

### AwaitAsyncCallback

Hands the dispatch back without settling it. Use this when the work outlives the RPC.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `async_ack_id` | The id you will call back with. Required. |
| `expected_completion_ms` | Declared, and not read by rimsky at this release |

An `AwaitAsyncCallback` with an empty `async_ack_id` fails the dispatch with `executor_protocol_violation` and the reason `await_async_missing_ack_id`.

Rimsky records the ack id durably, so a supervisor restart does not lose your callback. The deadlines that then govern the dispatch are the node's `max_quiet_period` and `max_runtime`, not `expected_completion_ms`.

### Tags are checked against your advertisement

Rimsky compares the `tags` on every settling outcome against the `declared_tags` from your capabilities handshake. A tag you did not declare turns the outcome into an error with the class `executor_protocol_violation`, the reason `undeclared_tag`, and the offending tag named. Declare every tag you emit.

Tags are load-bearing at run time, not decorative. Two subscribers filtering on different declared tags of the same sending node run selectively: the one matching the tag you emitted fires, the other does not.

## The async callback

When you return `AwaitAsyncCallback`, finish the dispatch by posting to the supervisor.

```
POST ${callback_url}/v1/callback/${async_ack_id}
Content-Type: application/json
```

The body is an `AsyncCallbackBody`: a JSON object with exactly one of `success`, `error`, or `park`. Each carries the same fields as the matching `Outcome` case. Park's `resume_at` is an RFC3339 string and is required.

```json
{"success": {"changed": true, "change_summary": "rows written", "attributes_delta": {"rows": 42}}}
```

Rules the supervisor enforces:

- A body with zero or more than one outcome set answers `400`, naming how many it found.
- A body that is not JSON answers `400` with `invalid json`.
- A `park` without `resume_at`, or with a `resume_at` that is not RFC3339, answers `400`.
- An unknown `async_ack_id` answers `404` with `unknown_async_ack_id`.

The `events` field (1) is reserved on `AsyncCallbackBody`. Do not send it. The legacy `{"type": "complete"|"blocked"|"errored"}` shape is gone; the supervisor answers `400` to it.

On success the supervisor answers `200` with an `ack_status`. Five values exist: `accepted`, `rejected_run_terminal`, `rejected_run_stale`, `rejected_run_parked`, and `rejected_unknown`. A rejected status means your callback arrived after the run moved on; the response then carries `current_node_run_id` when a successor run exists.

Under mutual TLS the supervisor requires a client certificate on the callback route, and it requires the same principal that received the dispatch. A mismatch answers `401`, and the ack id stays live for the right caller.

## Keepalive and attribute writeback

Two more routes are open to you for the length of a run. Both require the dispatch's `cancel_token` as a bearer token; without it they answer `401`.

```
POST ${callback_url}/v1/runs/${dispatch_id}/keepalive
Authorization: Bearer ${cancel_token}
```

Answers `204`. It bumps the run's progress clock and renews the expiry on every claim the run holds. Call it while long work is in flight so the quiet-period deadline does not fire. An unknown run answers `404` with `unknown_run_id`.

```
POST ${callback_url}/v1/runs/${dispatch_id}/attributes
Authorization: Bearer ${cancel_token}
Content-Type: application/json

{"attributes_delta": {"progress": 0.5}}
```

Answers `204` and merges the delta onto the run's attributes, bumping the progress clock as a keepalive does. An empty or missing `attributes_delta` answers `400`. A run that is neither running nor holding a claim answers `409` with `run_not_active` and the current state.

## Deadlines

Three deadlines govern a dispatch. A template author sets each per node, and an operator sets deployment-wide defaults under `dispatch_defaults`.

| Deadline | Node key | Default | What it bounds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Synchronous RPC | `sync_rpc_deadline` | 30s | How long rimsky waits on the `Execute` call |
| Quiet period | `max_quiet_period` | off | How long a dispatch may go without progress |
| Runtime | `max_runtime` | off | How long a dispatch may run in total |

Exceeding the synchronous deadline settles the node with the error class `executor_sync_timeout`. The quiet-period and runtime deadlines apply after you return `AwaitAsyncCallback`; a keepalive or an attribute writeback resets the quiet clock, and nothing resets the runtime clock. Both are measured in whole seconds, and a value under one second is a configuration error. Set either to `0` to disable it.

## The trace surface

`GetTrace` returns the whole trace for one `dispatch_id`. `StreamTrace` streams `TraceEvent` values for one `dispatch_id`.

`Trace` carries `dispatch_id`, `evicted`, `complete`, and `events`. Answer a dispatch id you have never seen, or one whose retention window has passed, with `evicted: true`, `complete: true`, and no events. That is the shape the conformance run checks.

Each `TraceEvent` carries `event_id`, `parent_event_id`, `timestamp`, `severity`, `category`, `message`, and an `attributes` struct. `Severity` takes `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, or `ERROR`.

`category` is free-form, but six categories carry required attributes:

| Category | Required attributes |
| --- | --- |
| `step_started` | `step_id` |
| `step_completed` | `step_id` |
| `step_failed` | `step_id`, `error` |
| `subcall_started` | `subcall_id`, `target` |
| `subcall_completed` | `subcall_id` |
| `tool_call` | `tool_name`, `arguments`, `result`, `duration_ms` |
| `error` | `error` |

## Proving it

Run the conformance suite against your endpoint:

```
rimsky conformance executor --endpoint grpc://localhost:9099 --check-observability
```

The suite refuses to start unless it can prove your executor is in stub mode, because its scenarios drive canned responses. Pass `--allow-live` to run against a live endpoint; stub-requiring scenarios then skip.

Stub mode is a mode your executor implements. In it, you read probe attributes off the request and return the canned outcome each one asks for:

| Attribute | What you return |
| --- | --- |
| `stub_probe: true` | `Success` with `attributes_delta` `{"stub": true}` |
| `probe_park: true` | `Park`, at `park_resume_at` when that attribute is set |
| `probe_async: true` | `AwaitAsyncCallback`, then call back |
| `probe_cancel: true` | Call back `cancel-observed`, then `cancel-acknowledged` |
| `stub_tags: [...]` | The named tags on the outcome |
| `_invalid` present | `Error`, for the malformed-shape scenario |

The nine scenarios are `execute_happy_path`, `attributes_serialization`, `malformed_attributes`, `park_emission`, `scratch_park_round_trip`, `tags_round_trip`, `async_handoff`, `async_callback_survives_restart`, and `cancel`. Select or exclude them with `--scenarios` and `--skip`.

`--check-observability` probes `Capabilities`, checks that a non-empty `expected_attributes_schema` parses as JSON, checks that no declared tag is empty, checks the evicted shape of `GetTrace` and `StreamTrace`, and drives one canned dispatch. Add `--retention-test-seconds N` to drive a dispatch, wait, and check that the trace evicted.

`rimsky conformance probe --endpoint <url>` runs the stub-mode probe alone.

## What the product does not do

The park probe attributes are yours to implement, not a platform feature. `probe_park`, `probe_cancel`, and `park_resume_at` register cleanly on any node against any executor, and they do nothing unless the executor honours them under its own stub-mode flag. The same holds for `stub_response`: a template author cannot exercise a graph offline by setting it, because honouring it is your choice and your operator's.
